historical_timeline.summary: Mother died; placed in an orphan asylum at 15.
Won the Apollo Theater amateur contest.
Health problems began; diabetes affected her eyes; cataract surgery, then touring more than 40 weeks a year.
Intensive care for heart trouble; quintuple-bypass heart surgery.
Spoke of missing the road during her convalescence.
Both legs amputated below the knee; created her charitable foundation.
Died at home in Beverly Hills.

claims.statement: Ella Jane Fitzgerald was born on April 25, 1917, in Newport News, Virginia, to Temperance and William Fitzgerald. Most biographies gave 1918, but her birth certificate and school records show 1917.
In 1932 her mother died suddenly of a heart attack; orphaned at 15, she was placed in the Colored Orphan Asylum in Riverdale, New York.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history from the cited source; age at death not given.

claims.statement: In 1934 she won an amateur contest at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, which brought her to the attention of the drummer and bandleader Chick Webb; she made her first recording with his band in 1935, and her 1938 swing version of the nursery rhyme "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" became her first hit.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her life as a performing singer anchors the modern social history.

claims.statement: She won the Grammy Award for Best Jazz Individual Performance in 1958 for Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Duke Ellington Song Book, and received the Kennedy Center award for lifetime achievement in 1979. She was known as America's first lady of song.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Achievement and identity, recorded as strengths.

claims.statement: She was awarded the National Medal of Freedom in 1992.
She began to have health problems during the 1970s; she had diabetes, which caused problems with her eyes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern diabetic retinopathy. The type of diabetes and its treatment were not made public.

claims.statement: In the 1970s, after cataract surgery, she returned to touring more than 40 weeks a year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the lens implants in the modern eye examination and for her touring life.

claims.statement: In 1986 she was admitted to intensive care for heart trouble and underwent quintuple-bypass heart surgery; the following year she was back onstage.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern coronary artery disease after bypass surgery the year before the index visit.

quintuple-bypass heart surgery; back onstage the following year

claims.statement: She had been suffering from diabetes and its circulatory system complications for many years before her death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern peripheral artery disease. Reported at her death; no fetched source dates the start of the circulatory complications.

claims.statement: In 1993 both of her legs were amputated below the knees because of complications of diabetes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only. The modern episode does not stage or predict this outcome.

source_links.locator: the effects of diabetes led to operations to remove both her legs

claims.statement: In 1993 she created and funded the Ella Fitzgerald Charitable Foundation, whose areas of interest include medical care and research with an emphasis on diabetes, vision problems, and heart disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as a strength and as the conditions she chose to name.

claims.statement: In 1989, asked how she spent her convalescence, she said: "Staying home and being bored. I miss the road. I miss going overseas."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public words, after the index date; they show what performing and travel meant to her.

claims.statement: She died at home in Beverly Hills, California, on June 15, 1996, at 79. The exact cause of death was not released; one public timeline attributes it to complications of diabetes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; recorded in one sentence.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Limb-, sight- and heart-protecting primary care for a 70-year-old touring singer with type 2 diabetes, peripheral artery disease with claudication, diabetic macular edema, and coronary bypass surgery the year before: the comprehensive diabetic foot examination (inspection, 10-g monofilament, vibration, pulses) with the ankle- and toe-brachial indices, IWGDF risk grading and a high-risk foot program with podiatry and stage footwear; prompt vascular surgery evaluation, supervised exercise therapy, and a clear plan for revascularization if symptoms limit her life; a high-intensity statin with ezetimibe to an LDL below 55 mg/dL, aspirin with low-dose rivaroxaban, and glucose-lowering medicines with cardiovascular and kidney benefit (empagliflozin, then semaglutide) in place of a sulfonylurea; retinal care with anti-VEGF injections; kidney monitoring; hypoglycemia safety on tour (insulin timing across time zones, a continuous glucose monitor, glucagon, and a show-day plan); and the equity and access steps that make this care reach her, on the ADA Standards of Care 1987, the IWGDF 1984 guidelines, the 1985 ACC/AHA lower extremity PAD guideline, and the CMID diabetes monograph.

problems.display: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral artery disease: cramping in both calves after about one and a half blocks of walking, worse on the right, easing within minutes of rest; no rest pain, wounds, or color change. Resting ankle-brachial index 0.62 right and 0.74 left, toe-brachial index 0.46 and 0.55; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses absent on the right and faint on the left. A1c 8.6% on metformin, glipizide and glargine, with low glucose readings (to 52 mg/dL) after late performances. Foot: protective sensation intact to the 10-g monofilament at all sites and to vibration; callus under the second metatarsal heads; hammer toes of the second and third toes; no ulcer (IWGDF risk category 2). hpi.narrative: Ms. Fitzgerald returns two weeks after her first visit and is seen by Dr. Okafor-Lane of vascular surgery on the same day. She stopped glipizide, moved glargine 24 units to the morning, and started empagliflozin 10 mg and atorvastatin 80 mg. Her continuous glucose monitor shows glucose between 70 and 180 mg/dL 58% of the time, time below 70 mg/dL 0.5%, with a lowest reading of 68 mg/dL after a long rehearsal, and no reading below 54 mg/dL; there have been no lows after shows. She has no burning or itching with urination and no muscle aches. Calf cramping still stops her after about one and a half blocks, more on the right; she has no rest pain or sores. Her right eye remains blurred; the retina clinic will see her next week.

assessment_plan.display: Type 2 diabetes with peripheral artery disease
assessment_plan.assessment: No lows below 54 mg/dL since glipizide was stopped and glargine was reduced and moved to the morning. Time in range is 58%; the usual goal is above 70%, or above 50% for an older adult at high risk of lows, and it should rise as empagliflozin takes effect. Dr. Okafor-Lane's arterial duplex shows an occluded right superficial femoral artery with flow restored above the knee and two open arteries to the foot, and a 50 to 69% narrowing of the left superficial femoral artery; no disease above the groin. She has lifestyle-limiting claudication without signs of a threatened limb, so supervised exercise and medicines come first
plan: Start rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily with aspirin 81 mg
Supervised exercise three times a week for twelve weeks, starting next week, with a home walking plan for tour weeks

assessment.display: Type 2 diabetes with peripheral artery disease
assessment.assessment: Femoropopliteal peripheral artery disease in both legs: a right superficial femoral artery occlusion and a moderate left superficial femoral artery stenosis, with good flow to the feet. She has lifestyle-limiting claudication without signs of chronic limb-threatening ischemia (no rest pain, wound, or gangrene), so the limb is not at immediate risk. The first steps are supervised exercise therapy and medical therapy, which improve walking and lower the risk of heart attack, stroke, and limb events. Revascularization is considered when claudication still limits her life after a trial of exercise and medicines, and urgently if a wound, rest pain, or color change appears. Because amputation is more common in people with diabetes, and more common still, and more often done without a vascular assessment first, in Black Americans and in people with less access to care, she should have a low threshold for prompt vascular review of any foot problem
